title: Odd-to-Even-Layer Switch of Spontaneous Excitonic State in $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ Thin Films
authors: Kaili Wang, Zhuowei Liu, Yuyang Mu, Zhujuan Li, Zhenjie Fan, Yu Gui, Xiaodong Qiu, Baigeng Wang, Rui Wang, Yi Zhang, Qi-Kun Xue
abstract: $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ is a candidate of high temperature excitonic condensates with spontaneous exciton formation in addition to its charge density wave (CDW). However, direct observation and manipulation of this electron-hole paring state formation is still lacking. Here, using varying-temperature angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (VT-ARPES), we observe a distinct odd-to-even-layer switch of spontaneous exciton state formation with the evident correlated band structure in $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ thin films. While the odd-layer $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ films show a sharp band structure in single-particle picture superimposed by CDW renormalization, in the even-layer $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ films, the full-filling valence band (VB) opens a distinct notch at the top, and the conductive band (CB) shows a significant extra signal extending above Fermi level with spectra broadening. These features indicate that the extra holes (notched VB) and electrons (broadening CB above Fermi level) form spontaneous excitons in even-layer $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$. Based on a correlated electron-hole model extracted from the tight-binding description, we reproduce the characterized band structures with spontaneous exciton formation, where the interlayer inter-band coupling in $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ plays a key role, which leads to an odd-to-even-layer switch of the excitonic state formation. Our results provide direct evidences of the spontaneous exciton formation, promising an excitonic condensate as versatile platform for realizing Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) and investigating novel correlated phenomena.
summary: This work investigates spontaneous exciton formation in $m{TiSe_{2}}$ thin films using VT-ARPES, revealing a distinct electronic switch between odd- and even-layer thicknesses. The evidence for excitons comes from spectral notches and broadening in even layers, which is theoretically explained by interlayer coupling within a correlated electron-hole model.
main_problem: The primary challenge is the direct observation and manipulation of the spontaneous exciton formation state in $m{TiSe_{2}}$, a material candidate for high-temperature excitonic condensates.
main_result: The study provides direct evidence of spontaneous exciton formation in even-layer $m{TiSe_{2}}$ films, characterized by a VB notch and CB broadening, which is linked to an odd-to-even-layer switch driven by interlayer coupling.
method: The research combines experimental measurements using Variable Temperature ARPES (VT-ARPES) with theoretical modeling based on a correlated electron-hole model.
model_or_system: The system is $m{TiSe_{2}}$ thin films grown on $m{SrTiO_{3}}(111)$. The theoretical framework involves modeling the excitonic instability using interlayer interband coupling within a tight-binding description.
key_observables: ARPES spectral features, specifically the VB notch opening in even layers and the CB broadening above the Fermi level, alongside temperature dependence of these features.
important_parameters: Layer thickness (odd vs. even), temperature (especially near 250 K), and the strength of interlayer inter-band coupling.
main_assumptions: The interpretation of spectral weight changes (notch/broadening) as direct evidence of spontaneous exciton formation, and the use of a correlated two-band model for theoretical reproduction.
figures_summary: Figures show ARPES spectra mapping the band structure for varying layer numbers (1L to 4L), highlighting the spectral changes in the VB and CB that differentiate odd and even layers.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from experimental observation (ARPES showing layer-dependent spectral changes) to theoretical modeling (using a correlated electron-hole model) to explain the observed odd-to-even-layer switch in excitonic behavior.
why_interesting: The study directly addresses excitonic condensation, a topic central to strongly correlated physics, and links it to measurable spectroscopic signatures (notch/broadening) that can be compared to theoretical predictions of excitonic instabilities.
